clue.text: Just left with twenty-five pounds to go round (no pressure)

indicators.note: the trimmed slang word has to go round the other letter, enclosing it
'no pressure' asks for the pressure symbol to be dropped from the word before

parts.note: a pony is British slang for twenty-five pounds sterling
P is the physics symbol for pressure

explanation.surface: Someone left with a small sum of money, hoping it stretches, without any stress.
explanation.walkthrough: PONY is British slang for £25; 'no pressure' removes its P, leaving ONY, which goes round L.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words work as adverbs meaning merely, as in 'just a minute' and 'only a minute'.

clue.text: Elaboration of dancer having supply nipped between partners?

indicators.note: the trimmed word sits between the two bridge players' letters

parts.note: in bridge North and South are partners, giving the compass letters S and N

indicators.note: nipped means the word's tip is cut off, losing its final letter

parts.note: to supply or kit out is to equip

explanation.surface: A dancing couple sharing what they have, someone pinched in between them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Partners' are the bridge pair South and North; EQUIP 'nipped' loses its last letter to give EQUI.
explanation.definitionFit: A spangle stitched on a dancer's costume is a decorative embellishment, an elaboration of the outfit.

clue.text: Agitate can

definitions.meaning: to agitate a liquid is to mix it with a spoon
the can is slang for prison, as is another four-letter word

explanation.surface: Stirring up trouble lands you in jail.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the verb to mix by moving a spoon; the other is old slang for jail.

clue.text: Teased Ryan wearing boy's cords

indicators.note: the boys' word is wearing the shuffled name inside it

parts.note: boy's read as 'boys', plural, gives lads

indicators.note: teased as in hair combed out, so the name's letters are tangled into a new order

explanation.surface: Ryan gets mocked for wearing another boy's corduroys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Teased' (as in combed-out hair) is the anagram signal and 'wearing' the container; 'cords' reads as corduroy trousers but means ropes.
explanation.definitionFit: Lanyards are cords worn round the neck or used on ships to hold things.

clue.text: Slash with power and produce tears

parts.note: a slash is British slang for urinating, as is a wee

explanation.surface: Cutting with force and bringing on the tears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slash' is not a cut but British slang for a pee.
explanation.definitionFit: To cry is to shed tears, so producing tears is crying.

clue.text: A feature of Noel's eyes in 26

definitions.meaning: Noel is Christmas, and small fruit-filled pastries are a seasonal staple of it
in Cockney rhyming slang of the East End, the phrase rhymes with and stands for eyes

explanation.surface: A man called Noel's eyes, as seen in east London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noel' looks like a man's name but means Christmas.
explanation.definitionFit: Small sweet pastries filled with dried fruit are Christmas fare, and the phrase is rhyming slang for eyes.

clue.text: Woman, always with uniform, turned into bloke

indicators.note: into says the turned letters go inside the word for a man

parts.note: a bloke is British slang for a man

indicators.note: turned means the pair of pieces before it are read backwards

parts.note: e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, meaning always
U is uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A woman who, with a uniform on, was always becoming a man.
explanation.walkthrough: E'ER plus U, 'turned', gives UREE, which goes 'into' MAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A female given name, so it can stand for a woman, as names often do in crosswords.

clue.text: Thief in 26 performing feat disrupted by grass

indicators.note: disrupted by says the shuffled letters are split open by the next piece
performing suggests the letters of the word after it put on a show, moved about

parts.note: taken as written
a lea is a grassy meadow

explanation.surface: A thief in east London, pulling off a feat, gets interrupted by an informer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Performing' turns FEAT into TEAF, 'disrupted by' LEA. 'Grass' tempts as an informer, which suits a thief, but here it is a meadow.
explanation.definitionFit: In Cockney rhyming slang the brewing leaf rhymes with and stands for a robber.

clue.text: Discussion held here's beneficial to rising character in Marathon

parts.note: something 'for' you is to your benefit

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means the letters are read upwards, backwards

parts.note: Marathon is in Greece, so the character is a Greek letter, mu

explanation.surface: Debate over whether running a marathon builds character.
explanation.walkthrough: MU, a Greek letter, read upwards in this down clue gives UM.
explanation.definitionFit: A public meeting place or online board where views are exchanged is where debate happens.

clue.text: Much water flowing after Oswald's killer curry in 26

indicators.note: after puts the river's name behind the killer's surname

parts.note: Jack Ruby shot Lee Harvey Oswald, assassin of President Kennedy
the Murray is Australia's longest river, a lot of flowing water

explanation.surface: A great deal of liquid running behind an infamous assassin, then a curry in east London.
explanation.walkthrough: Ruby Murray was a 1950s singer whose name became Cockney rhyming slang for curry.
explanation.definitionFit: In rhyming slang the singer's name rhymes with and stands for the spicy dish.

clue.text: See 27
Cockney's abruptly moving jacket

indicators.note: a Cockney speaker drops the final G of an -ing word

parts.note: jerking is moving with sudden starts

explanation.surface: A Londoner's jacket twitching about.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney speech famously drops the final G, so JERKING becomes the sleeveless garment.
explanation.definitionFit: A close-fitting, often sleeveless, leather coat for men, a kind of jacket.

clue.text: Soul artist the latest to invest amount of gold in US

parts.note: the ka is the soul or spirit in ancient Egyptian belief
RA is a Royal Academician, a crossword artist

indicators.note: the latest to arrive in a word is its final letter, taken here from invest

explanation.surface: A soul singer being the most recent to put money into American gold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The latest to invest' is the last letter of 'invest'. 'Soul artist' looks like a singer but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The American spelling of the measure of gold purity, twenty-fourths of pure metal.

clue.text: European gentle with ridicule over time in 26

indicators.note: over means the three pieces together are turned over, read backwards

parts.note: mild means gentle
to rib someone is to tease or ridicule them

explanation.surface: A mild European who has been mocked, in east London slang.
explanation.walkthrough: E + MILD + RIB 'over' reads backwards. Bird-lime is rhyming slang for time, as in a prison sentence ('doing bird').
explanation.definitionFit: The sticky trap substance rhymes with and stands for time, especially a prison stretch, in Cockney slang.

clue.text: Job in Germany camouflages fling

indicators.note: the phrase camouflages the word inside its run of letters

explanation.surface: A job in Germany covers up an affair.
explanation.definitionFit: A fling is a short spell of wild indulgence, and so is a spree of excess.

clue.text: He circulated tracks, given praise by audience primarily

parts.note: to laud is to praise

indicators.note: primarily picks the first letter of the word audience

explanation.surface: A man going round tracks, cheered on by the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: Niki Lauda was an Austrian Formula One world champion.
explanation.definitionFit: A racing driver literally went round circuits, a playful description of the Austrian champion.

clue.text: Victorian novel delivered by mouth in 26

definitions.meaning: Elizabeth Gaskell's 1855 novel of industrial England
Cockney rhyming slang, the two compass points rhyming with and standing for mouth

explanation.surface: A nineteenth-century book read aloud in east London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delivered by' is a link between the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaskell wrote a book of this title, and the compass phrase rhymes with mouth in rhyming slang.

clue.text: Female black grouse's warm at edges of hutch with little space

parts.note: to heat something is to warm it

indicators.note: edges of picks the first and last letters of hutch

parts.note: an en is a small printing space, half an em

explanation.surface: A female bird's hutch, cosy at the edges and cramped.
explanation.walkthrough: An en is a printer's unit of space, half an em.
explanation.definitionFit: A grouse, female of the heath-cock or black grouse, as dictionaries record.

clue.text: Literary critic finding unknown works in Derby perhaps

indicators.note: in places the unknown and the works inside the headgear

parts.note: a derby is a bowler, an example of a hat
Z is an algebraic unknown
lit, short for literature, is written works

explanation.surface: A critic discovers unidentified writings in the city of Derby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Derby' looks like the English city but is a bowler hat.
explanation.definitionFit: William Hazlitt was a Romantic-era essayist and critic of literature and drama.

clue.text: In 26, face snake and react stupidly

parts.note: a boa is a large snake

indicators.note: acting stupidly, the letters of react are jumbled into nonsense order

explanation.surface: Confronting a snake and panicking foolishly in east London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stupidly' rearranges REACT to TRACE. 'Face' looks like a verb, confront, but is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: In Cockney rhyming slang the Oxford–Cambridge rowing contest rhymes with and stands for face.

clue.text: Quadruped tiddler regularly checked in compound

parts.note: an ox is a four-legged animal

indicators.note: regularly checked means every other letter of tiddler is picked out

explanation.surface: An animal and a little fish routinely examined inside an enclosure.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking every second letter of 'tiddler' gives IDE.
explanation.definitionFit: Rust and similar substances are chemical compounds of oxygen with another element.

clue.text: It contains beat that's unknown, and it sometimes rhymes

indicators.note: contains says the two-letter word holds the next pieces inside

parts.note: It is sex appeal, abbreviated SA
to tan someone's hide is to beat them
Z is an algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: Something with a rhythm nobody knows, which occasionally rhymes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' as sex appeal (SA) is a crossword convention. 'Beat' reads as rhythm but means TAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A verse of a poem, which often, though not always, rhymes.

clue.text: Gloomy doctor probes causing annoyance

indicators.note: probes means the doctor's letters push into the next word

parts.note: sore can mean irritating, as a sore point
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's qualification

explanation.surface: A miserable doctor's examination is irritating.
explanation.definitionFit: Dark and dismal, both of mood and of colour.

clue.text: See 6
Band playing amid silence

indicators.note: amid places the role word inside the call for quiet

parts.note: sh is the call for silence
playing a role is appearing as it

explanation.surface: A group performing in hushed surroundings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Band' looks like a musical group but is a strip of cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A strip of fabric worn round the waist or over the shoulder is a band.

clue.text: Starving in 26, drive back with wine to accompany unopened cut of meat

indicators.note: unopened means the word loses its opening letter

parts.note: shank is a cut of meat from the leg

indicators.note: back means the word is read in reverse

parts.note: to ram is to drive forcefully
vin is French for wine

explanation.surface: A hungry Londoner rams wine down with a piece of meat.
explanation.walkthrough: Hank Marvin, guitarist of the Shadows, is rhyming slang for starving. SHANK 'unopened' gives HANK; RAM 'back' gives MAR.
explanation.definitionFit: The guitarist's name rhymes with and stands for very hungry in Cockney rhyming slang.

clue.text: A top sportsman upset FA

indicators.note: in a down entry upset means turned upside down, read backwards

parts.note: a dan is a top grade in judo or karate, or one who holds it

explanation.surface: A star athlete annoyed the Football Association.
explanation.walkthrough: 'FA' is not the Football Association but 'sweet FA', Fanny Adams: nothing at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweet Fanny Adams is British slang for nothing; the Spanish word for nothing is used the same way.

clue.text: Cut down on computer programs (half needed)

parts.note: re means on, concerning

indicators.note: only half needed means just the first two letters of the four

parts.note: apps are computer programs

explanation.surface: Reducing the number of computer programs by half.
explanation.definitionFit: To harvest a crop is to cut it down.

clue.text: Where's right for Londoner?

parts.note: on a map east lies to the right, so the right-hand part of London is the home of its Cockneys

explanation.surface: Asking which place suits someone from London.
explanation.walkthrough: The East End is the traditional Cockney district of London, home of the rhyming slang that runs through this puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: On a map, the eastern district of London is on the right, and it is the Cockney heartland.

clue.text: Yell about pots being ruined by edge of knife and fork in 26

indicators.note: about means the yell goes round the shuffled letters

parts.note: to roar is to yell

indicators.note: ruined pots are broken, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the edge of a word here is its first letter, from knife

explanation.surface: A cook yells as the pots are spoilt by a knife and fork in east London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being ruined' turns POTS into ASTPO, held 'about' by ROAR, then K from 'edge of knife'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Cockney rhyming slang the Sunday meat dish rhymes with and stands for the eating utensil.
